For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Trauma Processing Therapy: A Precision-Weighted Approach to Memory Reconsolidation

text.text: All authors contributed to the study conception and design.
All authors read and approved the final manuscript.
Ethics Approval Ethics approval was not required for this study.
This article does not involve human participants, their data, or biological material.
The clinical vignette is a composite of several clinical encounters; all identifying information has been changed, and it does not represent any one individual.
Consent to Participate Not applicable.
Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a frequent and debilitating consequence of trauma exposure.
It is associated with major problems in daily functioning, social relationships and overall quality of life (Jellestad et al., 2021).
text.formatted: It is associated with major problems in daily functioning, social relationships and overall quality of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Jellestad et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Current clinical guidelines recommend trauma-focused psychotherapies (e.g., prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, trauma-focused cognitive-behavioural therapy) as first-line treatment options, supported by strong empirical evidence and efficacy in different trauma populations (Foa et al., 2013; Rothbaum & Watkins, 2025).
text.formatted: Current clinical guidelines recommend trauma-focused psychotherapies (e.g., prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, trauma-focused cognitive-behavioural therapy) as first-line treatment options, supported by strong empirical evidence and efficacy in different trauma populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Foa et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Rothbaum & Watkins, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: PTSD is still a challenging condition to treat for many patients, especially those with chronic, complex or severe trauma-related symptoms (Karatzias et al., 2019).
text.formatted: PTSD is still a challenging condition to treat for many patients, especially those with chronic, complex or severe trauma-related symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Karatzias et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Many patients benefit from empirically supported psychotherapies, but the same limitations recur across studies.

Full remission is not achieved by many people, dropout rates are high, especially with exposure-based therapies, and relapse is common even in those who respond initially (Bradley et al., 2005; Najavits, 2015; Schottenbauer et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Full remission is not achieved by many people, dropout rates are high, especially with exposure-based therapies, and relapse is common even in those who respond initially <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bradley et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Najavits, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Schottenbauer et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This implies that the problem may not be in the delivery or enactment of therapy.
It may also indicate a more profound fundamental limitation in how existing therapies try to modify trauma-related memories and beliefs (Rothbaum & Watkins, 2025; Vervliet et al., 2013).
text.formatted: It may also indicate a more profound fundamental limitation in how existing therapies try to modify trauma-related memories and beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Rothbaum & Watkins, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Vervliet et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Part of this limitation stems from the fact that most trauma-focused therapies are primarily based on extinction learning.
Extinction does not erase the original traumatic memory.
In contrast, it produces new inhibitory learning that diminishes anxiety reactions under favourable conditions (Lebois et al., 2019; Schiller & Delgado, 2010).
text.formatted: In contrast, it produces new inhibitory learning that diminishes anxiety reactions under favourable conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Lebois et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Schiller & Delgado, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As the original representation of the threat is retained, traumatic reactions may be reactivated under conditions of stress, in different contexts or when environmental stimuli evoke the original trauma.
Treatments that rely on inhibitory learning, rather than changing the unpleasant memories themselves, might lead to relapse (Monfils & Holmes, 2018; Vervliet et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Treatments that rely on inhibitory learning, rather than changing the unpleasant memories themselves, might lead to relapse <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Monfils & Holmes, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Vervliet et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Memory reconsolidation is a different paradigm.
It implies that a consolidated memory may become labile for some time when reactivated, so that it can be updated before it is reconsolidated (Lee et al., 2017; Nader, 2015).
text.formatted: It implies that a consolidated memory may become labile for some time when reactivated, so that it can be updated before it is reconsolidated <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Lee et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Nader, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This would allow a change in the original traumatic memory, rather than creating a conflicting inhibitory memory.
However, the reliability and the limitations of reconsolidation-oriented therapies are still a matter of lively discussion (Phelps & Hofmann, 2019).
text.formatted: However, the reliability and the limitations of reconsolidation-oriented therapies are still a matter of lively discussion <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Phelps & Hofmann, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Scholars do not agree on the mechanisms of memory destabilisation, the conditions that promote reconsolidation and the process by which correction information is integrated into a reactivated memory trace (Beckers & Kindt, 2017; Bui & Milton, 2023; Kida, 2020; Treanor et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Scholars do not agree on the mechanisms of memory destabilisation, the conditions that promote reconsolidation and the process by which correction information is integrated into a reactivated memory trace <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Beckers & Kindt, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bui & Milton, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kida, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Treanor et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A recent narrative review likewise concludes that reconsolidation may operate as a shared mechanism of change across psychotherapies, while noting that its clinical use depends on timing, emotional regulation, and contextual boundary conditions (Ismaya et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A recent narrative review likewise concludes that reconsolidation may operate as a shared mechanism of change across psychotherapies, while noting that its clinical use depends on timing, emotional regulation, and contextual boundary conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Ismaya et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: One framework that might shed light on how memories are altered during reconsolidation is predictive processing.
From this point of view, the brain works as a stratified system that generates predictions.
It constantly updates its internal models by minimising differences between its expectations and the data it receives.
These mismatches are called prediction errors (Clark, 2013; Friston, 2012; Friston & Stephan, 2007).
text.formatted: These mismatches are called prediction errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clark, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Friston, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Friston & Stephan, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The central tenet of this approach is precision weighting, which determines the influence of prior beliefs on new sensory information.

Excessive precision in maladaptive threat expectations can shape the interpretation of experiences and sustain trauma-related symptoms, despite fresh experiences that may contradict them (Chamberlin, 2019).
text.formatted: Excessive precision in maladaptive threat expectations can shape the interpretation of experiences and sustain trauma-related symptoms, despite fresh experiences that may contradict them <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chamberlin, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This notion is becoming significant in computational psychiatry and in predictive-processing frameworks of PTSD (Kaye & Krystal, 2020; Kube et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This notion is becoming significant in computational psychiatry and in predictive-processing frameworks of PTSD <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kaye & Krystal, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kube et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Predictive-processing frameworks elucidate the persistence of maladaptive expectations, while reconsolidation theories delineate the conditions under which memories may be revised (Lee et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Predictive-processing frameworks elucidate the persistence of maladaptive expectations, while reconsolidation theories delineate the conditions under which memories may be revised <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Lee et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, neither model adequately explains how corrective experiences should be incorporated into traumatic memories in therapy.
To address this gap, the present manuscript proposes Trauma Processing Therapy (TPT), a conceptual therapeutic approach that integrates memory reconsolidation and predictive processing.

Preliminary case-level documentation of TPT exists for prolonged grief disorder treated in a single session (Ardian, 2025) and for complex PTSD with treatment-resistant depression treated over six sessions (Octaviani et al., 2026).

text.text: TPT focuses on the creation of precisionweighted prediction discrepancies during the period of reconsolidation.
The aim is to increase the likelihood that the corrective information alters the original trauma representation, rather than being stored separately.
This is based on the data that prediction error is essential for destabilisation of fear memories (Sevenster et al., 2013).

text.text: TPT is a flexible closed-loop system in which each intervention is shaped by ongoing patient feedback.
TPT is not empirically supported.
The only clinical reports to date are these two uncontrolled single cases (Ardian, 2025; Octaviani et al., 2026), which are preliminary and cannot establish efficacy or mechanism.

text.text: It is a theory driven, operationalised framework which generates testable hypotheses for future research.
Its main argument is that lasting trauma recovery may require systematic manipulation of precision-weighted prediction errors during reconsolidation windows to update maladaptive trauma memories.
TPT is thus an extension of previous reconsolidation-based methods.
It offers a model for clinicians to use, links mechanisms of memory updating with the theory of predictive processing, and is empirically falsifiable and refinable.
The free-energy principle suggests that organisms survive by proactively minimising uncertainty about their environment (Friston, 2012).
text.formatted: The free-energy principle suggests that organisms survive by proactively minimising uncertainty about their environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Friston, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Organisms cannot directly access the hidden causes of their sensory inputs, and instead must use internal generative models to infer what is happening in the world (Friston et al., 2013; Friston & Stephan, 2007; Pezzulo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Organisms cannot directly access the hidden causes of their sensory inputs, and instead must use internal generative models to infer what is happening in the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Friston et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Friston & Stephan, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Pezzulo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The brain is, in this view, a prediction-making system.
It is always predicting sensory events and comparing these predictions with incoming information (Barrett & Simmons, 2015; Clark, 2013; Friston, 2012).
text.formatted: It is always predicting sensory events and comparing these predictions with incoming information <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barrett & Simmons, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Clark, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Friston, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, survival requires more than a reaction to stimuli.
It also depends on maintaining and updating internal models that predict environmental conditions well (Friston et al., 2010; Friston et al., 2013).
text.formatted: It also depends on maintaining and updating internal models that predict environmental conditions well <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Friston et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Friston et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than recording external reality, perception is an active process of inference used for predictive processing (Clark, 2013).
text.formatted: Rather than recording external reality, perception is an active process of inference used for predictive processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clark, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The brain constantly hypothesises the causes of sensory experience (Friston et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The brain constantly hypothesises the causes of sensory experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Friston et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: It uses prediction errors, the differences between expectations and sensory evidence, to update and refine these hypotheses (Feldman & Friston, 2010; Hohwy, 2012).
text.formatted: It uses prediction errors, the differences between expectations and sensory evidence, to update and refine these hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Feldman & Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hohwy, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The brain is not able to compute surprise per se, as this would require knowledge of the probability of a sensory input under all its possible causes (Friston et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The brain is not able to compute surprise per se, as this would require knowledge of the probability of a sensory input under all its possible causes <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Friston et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Uncertainty, which is surprise averaged over time, cannot be calculated directly.
The theory instead takes a computational stance, regarding variational free energy as a statistical quantity that the brain can compute from its own model (Friston et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The theory instead takes a computational stance, regarding variational free energy as a statistical quantity that the brain can compute from its own model <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Friston et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Surprise is upper bounded by variational free energy, so low free energy also implies low surprise (Friston, 2012; Friston et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Surprise is upper bounded by variational free energy, so low free energy also implies low surprise <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Friston, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Friston et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: There are two ways in which free energy can be reduced when there is a prediction error.

The brain can either update its internal model so that it predicts better, or it can act on the world to change its sensory input so that the input fits the model's predictions (Friston, 2012; Friston et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The brain can either update its internal model so that it predicts better, or it can act on the world to change its sensory input so that the input fits the model's predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Friston, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Friston et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Perception and learning are the first route; the second is action.
All three can therefore be seen as examples of the same basic process of free-energy minimisation (Friston, 2012; Friston et al., 2010).
text.formatted: All three can therefore be seen as examples of the same basic process of free-energy minimisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Friston, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Friston et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In this model, perception is a never-ending loop between predictions and prediction errors.
Predictions shape perception and prediction errors correct predictions when they do not fit the sensory evidence (Clark, 2013; Hohwy, 2012).
text.formatted: Predictions shape perception and prediction errors correct predictions when they do not fit the sensory evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clark, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hohwy, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This exchange enables the brain to improve its models of the environment (Clark, 2013).
text.formatted: This exchange enables the brain to improve its models of the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clark, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In a more general sense, cognition can be thought of as a process that is centred on prediction, updating models and reducing uncertainty (Pezzulo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In a more general sense, cognition can be thought of as a process that is centred on prediction, updating models and reducing uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Pezzulo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Changing priors is costly, so they cannot be changed very often.
Thus, the brain must decide whether an observation should or should not change a prior.
This is done by estimating how much each prediction error should update the current model.
This is called precision weighting.
It decides which mismatches are significant signals for updates and which are noise.
Precision weighting may be a key mechanism through which trauma distorts predictive inference as it regulates the trade-off between keeping a model stable and revising it.
For predictive processing, perception is not just a matter of detecting sensory inputs.
The brain also evaluates the importance of each input for inference.
Sensory signals vary in reliability, so prediction errors carry different amounts of evidence and cannot all be treated the same way (Feldman & Friston, 2010; Friston, 2022).
text.formatted: Sensory signals vary in reliability, so prediction errors carry different amounts of evidence and cannot all be treated the same way <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Feldman & Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Friston, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the brain estimates the confidence or precision of each prediction error before deciding whether to update its generative model (Friston, 2022; Friston et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Thus, the brain estimates the confidence or precision of each prediction error before deciding whether to update its generative model <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Friston, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Friston et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: More formally, precision is the inverse variance of a signal.
It captures the expected reliability of incoming information, and the strength of prediction errors in updating belief (Feldman & Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: It captures the expected reliability of incoming information, and the strength of prediction errors in updating belief <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Feldman & Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Precision weighting enables high-precision prediction errors to drive learning and revision of the model, and low precision errors are considered noise (Feldman & Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: Precision weighting enables high-precision prediction errors to drive learning and revision of the model, and low precision errors are considered noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Feldman & Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In this framework, precision acts as a gain-control mechanism that determines the salience of mismatches between prediction and sensation (Feldman & Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: In this framework, precision acts as a gain-control mechanism that determines the salience of mismatches between prediction and sensation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Feldman & Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Precision must be allocated selectively among competing signals; it is not evenly spread (Friston et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Precision must be allocated selectively among competing signals; it is not evenly spread <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Friston et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This leads to attenuation of less relevant signals, and the inference is dominated by signals of higher precision (Friston, 2022).
text.formatted: This leads to attenuation of less relevant signals, and the inference is dominated by signals of higher precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Friston, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This selective allocation provides a predictive-processing account of attention, which can be understood as optimising precision to particular sources of information (Feldman & Friston, 2010; Hohwy, 2012).
text.formatted: This selective allocation provides a predictive-processing account of attention, which can be understood as optimising precision to particular sources of information <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Feldman & Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hohwy, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Sensory attenuation works in the opposite direction: it is the active down-weighting of signals that are less informative or less relevant to behaviour (Idei et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Sensory attenuation works in the opposite direction: it is the active down-weighting of signals that are less informative or less relevant to behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Idei et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Perception is thus a function of both the information available and the weighting of that information (Hohwy, 2012).
text.formatted: Perception is thus a function of both the information available and the weighting of that information <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hohwy, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: One consideration in setting the precision weighting is statistical reliability, but so is the cost of being wrong.
Threat, harm and physiological integrity signals are given more weight from an adaptive point of view, because errors in these domains may endanger survival (Van den Bergh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Threat, harm and physiological integrity signals are given more weight from an adaptive point of view, because errors in these domains may endanger survival <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Van den Bergh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, threat-related cues often receive a higher weighting than their reliability alone would warrant, and have a stronger influence on perception, learning and behaviour (Chamberlin, 2019).
text.formatted: Thus, threat-related cues often receive a higher weighting than their reliability alone would warrant, and have a stronger influence on perception, learning and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chamberlin, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This bias is a functional trade-off: the cost of missing real danger is greater than the cost of over-estimating it (Van den Bergh et al., 2020).

text.text: Seen in that light, trauma is easier to understand.

Trauma-related disturbances may arise when threat predictions are resistant to updating and continue to influence perception, attention and behaviour long after the original threat has passed (Kube et al., 2020; Lyndon & Corlett, 2020).
text.formatted: Trauma-related disturbances may arise when threat predictions are resistant to updating and continue to influence perception, attention and behaviour long after the original threat has passed <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kube et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Lyndon & Corlett, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: That is because of two features of predictive processing.
First, threat predictions may be more precise than the evidence on which they are based (Van den Bergh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: First, threat predictions may be more precise than the evidence on which they are based <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Van den Bergh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Even when there is evidence of safety, fear of danger pervades perceptions (Chamberlin, 2019).
text.formatted: Even when there is evidence of safety, fear of danger pervades perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chamberlin, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Second, at all levels of the cortical hierarchy, free energy is minimised (Edwards et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Second, at all levels of the cortical hierarchy, free energy is minimised <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Edwards et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, minimising prediction error at one level may conflict with expectations and goals at a higher level, and this conflict underlies resistance to model revision (Van de Maele et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Thus, minimising prediction error at one level may conflict with expectations and goals at a higher level, and this conflict underlies resistance to model revision <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Van de Maele et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This implies that a belief can be maintained despite contradictory evidence, since accepting that evidence would increase error elsewhere in the hierarchy (Krupnik, 2020).

text.text: Neural defence systems adapt when they predict danger accurately, but overly exact expectations of threat may persist after the threat has passed, and maladaptive beliefs may arise (Meacham & Bergstrom, 2016).

text.text: For predictive processing, a hyperprecise prior is a belief that is held more confidently than the evidence warrants (Krupnik, 2020; Lawson et al., 2014).

text.text: Belief updating depends on the relative precision of priors and prediction errors, so a hyperprecise prior might resist updating when new evidence is given lower precision (Feldman & Friston, 2010; Friston, 2022).

text.text: Danger expectations may thus continue to dominate even when safety information contradicts them.
In this way, the precision-weighting mechanisms that normally support learning could also safeguard maladaptive beliefs from correction (Lawson et al., 2014; Wilkinson et al., 2017).

text.text: This resistance may help explain why some trauma-and fear-related symptoms are hard to treat.

If threat-related priors are hyper-precise, extinction learning may be less effective because strongly held expectations of danger may override safety information (Fujimoto, 2026; Vervliet et al., 2013).

text.text: Traumatic memories may be especially susceptible to this kind of resistance.
They are encoded under conditions of high emotional and physiological arousal, which tends to increase the vividness and confidence of memory (Kensinger, 2009).

text.formatted: They often have a sense of nowness about them: the event is experienced as if it is happening now rather than being recalled as past <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brewin et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This breadth, coupled with high precision, might make them immune to change by ordinary experience.
The hierarchy gives one more reason.
A prediction error updates a representation mainly at the level at which that prediction is formed (Friston, 2022).

text.text: A person can know they are safe and still feel unsafe.
This may be why cognitive reassurance fails, as it does not address the prediction errors that feed lower-level threat expectations (Fujimoto, 2026).

text.text: These points suggest the main proposal of this framework: the modification of a hyperprecise traumatic prior may require corrective prediction errors that match the original representation in content and strength, along the dimensions in which it is encoded (Krupnik, 2020).

text.text: Because traumatic priors are sensory, emotional and meaning-based, corrective experiences that are too narrow, too weak or at the wrong hierarchical level may not challenge the representation as a whole.
The rest of the parts not addressed will still be precise and continue stabilising the larger trauma model.
We term this a clinical 'lock-in' whereby the trauma representation persists despite repeated evidence to the contrary.

From a predictive-processing perspective, one reason that trauma can be difficult to treat is that traumatic memories might serve as highly precise and broadly distributed predictive models, rather than as simple associations (Lyndon & Corlett, 2020).

text.text: One explanation may lie in the mechanism of extinction learning.
Extinction does not seem to erase a fear memory.
It creates a new inhibitory safety association that competes with the original threat memory, which is preserved (Lebois et al., 2019; Schiller & Delgado, 2010; Sosa, 2022).

text.text: 3PI provides a clear but general, taxonomic account of the inferential goals of psychotherapy.
For instance, it describes exposure as revision of the model by accumulation of disconfirmed negative expectations (Foa & McLean, 2015).

text.text: The account does not do full justice to the neurobiological difference between extinction learning and direct prior modification.

If extinction creates a parallel, context-dependent safety prior that competes with the threat representation (Maren et al., 2013), then broad predictive-processing frameworks may fail to fully explain relapse via spontaneous recovery and renewal (de Jong et al., 2018; Foa & McLean, 2015).

text.text: Thus, a more explicit mechanism of therapeutic updating may be useful.
Like 3PI, TPT assumes that psychopathology is sustained by overly precise priors and that model updating is required for therapeutic change.
TPT, unlike 3PI, distinguishes between extinction learning and memory reconsolidation.

In TPT, uncalibrated exposure alone may not be sufficient to change a hyperprecise, multidimensional traumatic prior, because the corrective information may not match the prior in scope or hierarchical level.
The system can then resolve the mismatch by creating a secondary safety prior that lives alongside the original threat model.
TPT has a specific procedure for performing this updating.
Instead of building prediction error through repetition, it deliberately creates an inferential crisis.

It compresses the traumatic prior into a Dominant Affective State (DAS), identifies and strengthens a Corrective Affective Prediction (CAP), and then activates both simultaneously within the short window in which the prior is thought to remain labile.
The aim is to update the source representation directly and to translate principles of predictive processing into a concrete clinical procedure that can be tested.
Reconsolidation is another pathway because it affects the original memory representation.
When a memory is reactivated under appropriate conditions it can enter a short unstable state in which it can be modified prior to restabilisation (Kida, 2020; Nader, 2015).

text.text: This has two clinical implications for therapy: to induce prediction errors that are proportional with the extent and specificity of the trauma representation, and to provide corrective information within the narrow time window when the memory is labile (Beckers & Kindt, 2017; Bui & Milton, 2023; Milton et al., 2023).

text.text: Mechanistically, this framework suggests that trauma therapy might involve three core tasks: reactivating the traumatic prior, generating prediction errors of sufficient magnitude, and delivering corrective information while the prior is still labile.
TPT attempts to achieve this via a closed-loop adaptive process.
With each therapeutic pass, feedback in the form of changes in distress, emotional state, or resistance is used to modify the next intervention.
In this sense TPT is more a decision-making algorithm than a fixed sequence of steps, and its stages are recurring components.
The protocol controls timing via its sequence, pace and collision parameters.
An adaptive branch only deals with obstacle beliefs when they occur.
Dominant Affective State (DAS) is a very important operation in the protocol.
This operation is meant to respond to the problem that this framework defines as the central one: the scope of the traumatic past.

From this point of view, trauma is not so much a single memory as a high dimensional network in which sensory details, interpersonal information, bodily states, temporal features, and inferred meanings are conjoined and specified (Kearney & Lanius, 2022).
text.formatted: From this point of view, trauma is not so much a single memory as a high dimensional network in which sensory details, interpersonal information, bodily states, temporal features, and inferred meanings are conjoined and specified <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kearney & Lanius, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Trying to rework the entire composite at once can overwhelm the patient, and one corrective experience is unlikely to hit every dimension at once.
The DAS tries to make the traumatic past manageable by reducing its dimensional complexity.
This can be thought of as a kind of dimensionality reduction, in which the protocol collapses the broad prior into a single, all-encompassing affective-cognitive node.

The node is multimodal and can integrate interoceptive states, language and conceptual meaning, for example a somatic state of constriction together with the belief "I am powerless" (Lindquist et al., 2015; Oosterwijk et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The node is multimodal and can integrate interoceptive states, language and conceptual meaning, for example a somatic state of constriction together with the belief "I am powerless" <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Lindquist et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Oosterwijk et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: It provides the therapist with a target against which a commensurate prediction error can be generated.
The therapist can access the DAS through a dominant feeling or dominant core belief, using questions such as "What is the dominant feeling right now?"
or "What do you believe about yourself in that situation?"
Sometimes patients answer questions about feelings with a belief like "I am worthless" or "I am powerless."
These are not names of feelings, but are still considered the DAS.
In TPT, feelings and beliefs are two access points to one affectivecognitive configuration, thus attending to one may activate the other.
This is consistent with evidence that body feelings and thoughts share distributed neural networks (Oosterwijk et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This is consistent with evidence that body feelings and thoughts share distributed neural networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Oosterwijk et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Another advantage of compression is serialisation.
The DAS is one integrated affectivecognitive node at one level of processing.
So, each treatment cycle works on one node and the patient does not have to hold the whole traumatic composite in awareness at once.
This may mitigate the risk of defensive precision spikes and permit the updating to progress through manageable, closed-loop iterations.

As the prediction error at one DAS node is resolved, conditional probabilities across the wider network may change and the next highly weighted dimension is then more likely to become salient, for example a schema of worthlessness that emerges after fear subsides.
The protocol aims to iteratively revise the entire traumatic representation across treatment, but each cycle is manageable.
Distress is measured by Subjective Units of Distress (SUD) on a scale of 0 to 10 Gurwitch & Warner-Metzger, 2022).
text.formatted: Distress is measured by Subjective Units of Distress (SUD) on a scale of 0 to 10 <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Gurwitch & Warner-Metzger, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The SUD rating is not the intensity of the DAS, but the overall distress in the memory being processed.
In TPT, SUD is a stand-in for the precisionweighted prediction error, experienced as interoceptive or affective surprise.
This is consistent with interoceptive accounts of emotion, whereby emotional experience is described as a reflection of the brain's inferences about bodily states (Seth, 2013).
text.formatted: This is consistent with interoceptive accounts of emotion, whereby emotional experience is described as a reflection of the brain's inferences about bodily states <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Seth, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Prior precision is a latent construct that is not available to therapist or patient.
Repeated SUD ratings across cycles are used to check whether the precision of the traumatic prior is being corrected over time.
Distress is expected to increase briefly during collision events as prediction error is generated and this increase should not be read as clinical deterioration.
This is why the SUD is rated only at the end of the activation sequence.
A decreasing SUD over cycles may be indicative of revision.
A high SUD indicates an unresolved cycle, which might indicate an inert response (insufficient updating) or a resistant response (defensive impedance).
There are two limits.
SUD is a reflective, reportable judgement and so only provides indirect access to subpersonal predictionerror dynamics.
Nor, as an ordinal clinical scale, does it estimate the formal variational quantities of computational theory.
Having isolated the Dominant Affective State (DAS), the next task is to determine the direction from which a prediction error can be generated and to identify a candidate corrective prediction.

The protocol does this with two operational devices: the Unmet Affective Prediction The aim is to map the inferential structure of the active traumatic prior, and to locate where corrective information can enter.
Typically, a UAP is elicited by prompts such as "What does this feeling require?"
The stated need is not addressed by the protocol.
Asking what the feeling "wants" is a way of finding the conceptual boundary of the DAS, the dimension along which the affective state is defined by contrast with its opposite.
This is the axis that is likely to be most in conflict with the current prediction.
It is thus the direction in which the prediction error is expected to be generated.
The RSQ then asks about the affective state that would occur if the UAP were already fulfilled, with prompts such as "If [the UAP] were fulfilled, how would you feel?"
The answer is a candidate CAP.
The RSQ describes the corrective state as one that is already in force.
The objective of this framing is to reduce the likelihood of instant rejection of the corrective state "by habitual cognitive filters."
The patient need not believe the state is true, only to access its affective consequences.
This is a proposed mechanism of the protocol, not an empirically observed effect.
The RSQ also decides if a collision is allowed to go ahead.
If it produces an affective state that is significantly different from the DAS, the protocol moves to build and fortify the CAP.
If it produces no change, or simply reproduces the original affective state, this is taken as a sign that in this direction there is no usable prediction error.
Then the protocol does not generate a collision.
It looks back at the UAP and looks for another way.
Protective-supportive (soothed, accompanied, defended, helped) and agentic (fight back, brave, capable, empowered) are two broad directions of the UAP and RSQ.
The protocol utilises both.
If the work remains only on the protective-supportive side, a reduction in SUD may be only downregulation: the patient feels calmer, but the prior has not been corrected.
The inclusion of the agentic side is to ensure that a reduction in SUD can also indicate correction via prediction error.
Because SUD cannot tell us which of these has happened, correction is best judged by symptom outcomes, as lasting improvement may reflect the generalisation of a revised prior.
If the patient cannot name a UAP, the therapist may offer candidates.
To reduce the risk of leading the patient, the therapist always offers contrasting options, never options in the same direction.

For example, the therapist may provide a protective and an agentic choice, or a choice that focuses on the outside world (other people or the situation) and one that focuses on the patient's inner state.
The patient chooses the option that fits or rejects all of them and RSQ tests the chosen option.
The RSQ is contradicted by the expectation evoked by the CAP.
When the RSQ and this expectation are brought into contact, the resulting conflict is expected to generate the prediction error needed for revision.
The CAP is not fixed and can be improved or replaced, provided that it continues to evoke an expectation that contradicts the DAS.
What matters is not its specific content, but whether it challenges the dominant prior.
The UAP, RSQ and CAP are not always based only on the patient answers.
Alternatively, they may be generated in the course of discussion between patient and therapist.
The patient's answer may be derived from the same prior that gives rise to the symptoms and a CAP based only on that answer may then fail to contradict the DAS.
In these instances, the therapist may need to guide the CAP, for example from the protective-supportive end to the agentic end, or the reverse.
The RSQ often first yields a weak CAP.
Due to the low precision, it may not be able to compete with the high precision DAS that has long-organized experience (Lawson et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Due to the low precision, it may not be able to compete with the high precision DAS that has long-organized experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Lawson et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The protocol does not therefore go directly to collision.
First, it uses amplification, which progressively increases the precision and experiential weight of the CAP until it is strong enough to generate prediction error.
Amplification includes imagery that is not therapist-guided (Holmes et al., 2008), recall of congruent autobiographical experiences, and self-talk.
text.formatted: Amplification includes imagery that is not therapist-guided <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Holmes et al., 2008)</ref>, recall of congruent autobiographical experiences, and self-talk.

text.text: The goal is to transform the CAP from a tentative possibility into an experientially salient prediction that can hold its own against the established prior.
Imagery is developed only after the RSQ has identified a CAP that is truly different from the DAS.
A corrective prediction that is weak, imprecise, or not consistent with the target prior is likely to be dominated by the DAS and produce insufficient prediction error to be revised.
Amplification is meant to lower this risk.
The collision is more likely to challenge the dominant prior than to amplify it.
After the collision, the patient is asked to go back to the original memory and to recall Calibration is therefore qualitative: it tests for signs of an update.
Non-revision can take two forms, inert or resistant (Table 2).
text.formatted: Non-revision can take two forms, inert or resistant (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: They are different processes and require different responses, so the next step taken depends on why updating failed.
Active objections appear: an obstacle belief openly rejects or opposes the corrective state.
The corrective prediction is absent, not precise enough, or misdirected, so no meaningful mismatch is generated.

A cross-level conflict may be present: revising the lower-order prior would conflict with a higher-order prior that is also held with high precision, such as identity, self-coherence, or moral commitment (Van den Bergh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A cross-level conflict may be present: revising the lower-order prior would conflict with a higher-order prior that is also held with high precision, such as identity, self-coherence, or moral commitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Van den Bergh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Intensify or redirect the intervention: deepen the predictive collision, refine the DAS, re-navigate the UAP, or build a higherprecision CAP.
Pause the predictive collision and shift the therapeutic focus to the obstacle belief, which becomes the primary target for revision.
An inert response treated as resistance may be a lost chance for revision.
A resistant response pressed may consolidate the defence.
The protocol's main calibration task is therefore to tell the two apart.
Evaluation of a cycle is based on three parameters: change in SUD, change in type of dominant affect, and presence/absence of obstacle beliefs.
Together, they classify each cycle as either a revision or one of the two forms of non-revision.
These indicators require clinical judgement to read.
The most obvious sign of revision would be a drop in SUD, but this could be due to down-regulation (see Stage Two).
Changing the type of DAS does not have a fixed meaning and is read according to context.
A shift from one negative affect to another may point to a hidden part of the broader affective configuration that is coming into being through serialisation.

In patients with emotional numbing or dissociation, the appearance of a specific, identifiable affect for the first time may in itself be a sign of progress, in that it may indicate that an attenuated affective channel has regained sufficient precision to enter conscious awareness (Vaage-Kowalzik et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In patients with emotional numbing or dissociation, the appearance of a specific, identifiable affect for the first time may in itself be a sign of progress, in that it may indicate that an attenuated affective channel has regained sufficient precision to enter conscious awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Vaage-Kowalzik et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The per-cycle revision criterion is permissive by design: in most cases either a decrease in SUD or a change in affect type suffice to satisfy it.
It has a functional purpose: it provides information that determines the next cycle.
The protocol also includes a mechanical safety.

The protocol is never applied ad infinitum with no signs of updating, because if the SUD does not decrease for three consecutive cycles, the therapist stops the algorithmic application and starts direct inquiry.

The session is completed when three simultaneous conditions are met: (1) SUD is zero; (2) there is no negative affect; and ( 3 These three conditions in combination may suggest the loss of sensory immediacy and the location of the event in the past.

text.text: In TPT they are interpreted as signs that revision has made the prior less precise, rather than by suppression alone.
Obstacle beliefs are a contingent target, not part of the routine sequence of stages.

They seem to be a resistant form of non-revision: the system is activated by prediction error but does not assimilate it, and the patient denies the corrective state in a coherent way (Yon et al., 2018), with responses like "that could never happen" or "it would not be allowed."
text.formatted: They seem to be a resistant form of non-revision: the system is activated by prediction error but does not assimilate it, and the patient denies the corrective state in a coherent way <ref type="bibr">(Yon et al., 2018)</ref>, with responses like "that could never happen" or "it would not be allowed."

text.text: Conversely, an inert response does not register a meaningful mismatch.
Obstacle beliefs therefore actively object.

An obstacle belief becomes a therapeutic target only when it is actively blocking revision, either by preventing a workable corrective prediction from forming or by stopping a collision that is already underway.
Beliefs that do not interfere with updating are left untouched.
In TPT, a blocking belief is considered to be a different hyperprecise prior at a higher hierarchical level than the trauma representation being processed.

Revision of trauma history may threaten coherence of identity, disrupt an established affective function, or conflict with a belief that renders the corrective state seemingly forbidden (Ecker & Bridges, 2020; Miller et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Revision of trauma history may threaten coherence of identity, disrupt an established affective function, or conflict with a belief that renders the corrective state seemingly forbidden <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Ecker & Bridges, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Miller et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The obstacle belief itself is a prior, and is processed with the same architecture as the original target.
Instead of intensifying the collision, the therapist stops it, for continued pressure against a defended prior can reinforce the defence.
The obstacle belief is then compressed into a separate DAS and goes through the same closed loop (DAS → UAP → RSQ → CAP → Collision).
When the belief no longer hinders revision, the protocol reverts to the initial target.
TPT is applied rapidly, so that prediction error can be delivered when memory is assumed to be labile during the reconsolidation window.
For some patients this pace may be unbearable.
So, overwhelm needs to be differentiated from resistance.
Processing stops immediately and treatment returns to the previous phase which was not finished.

The vignette in Section 3 describes a stabilised patient with an uncomplicated course, so the protocol's safety and efficacy cannot be generalised to unstabilized, complex, developmental or dissociative cases.
In a resistant reaction, the patient coherently denies the corrective state, remaining present, reflective and open to dialogue.
Overwhelm is a failure of regulatory capacity.

It can take the form of affective surges that cannot be settled, re-experiencing rather than recollection, or loss of dual awareness, when the patient can no longer be with the memory and anchored in the present at the same time (Beutler et al., 2022; Corrigan et al., 2010; Ford & Courtois, 2009).
text.formatted: It can take the form of affective surges that cannot be settled, re-experiencing rather than recollection, or loss of dual awareness, when the patient can no longer be with the memory and anchored in the present at the same time <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beutler et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Corrigan et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Ford & Courtois, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The protocol handles the resistant response with the obstacle belief as the new target.

Overwhelm is managed outside of the protocol: The processing stops and the treatment is returned to grounding and stabilisation until the patient is back within his/her window of tolerance (Beutler et al., 2022; Corrigan et al., 2010; Ford & Courtois, 2009).

text.text: This distinction needs to be made in the moment as holding the material, as is done for resistance, may exacerbate dysregulation in a patient who is overwhelmed.
Overwhelm indicates that the prerequisites for processing are not yet in place.

TPT is an intervention in the processing phase of a phase-oriented model of trauma treatment, in which safety, affect-regulation capacity and a secure therapeutic alliance are established first (Cloître et al., 2011; Karatzias et al., 2019).

text.text: This vignette is a composite of several clinical encounters, with all identifying information changed, and does not represent any one individual.
This is done to show how the protocol is executed.
Ms.
A was an adult female who had intrusive re-experiencing of a past trauma.
The memory felt as though it were happening in the present, and it was accompanied by an abiding sense of worthlessness.
After she finished the stabilisation phase of trauma treatment, we began the processing.
The narrative below tracks the order in which dominant affective states emerged and were revised during the session.
It is presented as selected annotated interchanges.
The decrease in distress is shown to be linear for ease of teaching.
In practice, work with severe PTSD often follows non-linear trajectories, with temporary increases in distress during activation and cycles that are initially inert (Hayes et al., 2007).
text.formatted: In practice, work with severe PTSD often follows non-linear trajectories, with temporary increases in distress during activation and cycles that are initially inert <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hayes et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The memory was reactivated in third person perspective and rated for intensity at the beginning.
In the following exchanges T = therapist and C = client.
T: When you hold this event in mind, what does it say about you?
C: That I am worthless.
T: Say the words, "I am worthless."
From 1, completely false, to 7, completely true, how true do these words feel right now?
(baseline VoC) C: Six.
T: As you hold the event in mind, with 0 neutral and 10 most distressing, where are you?
(reactivation; SUD) C: Ten.
T: At ten, what is the most distressing feeling?
(DAS) T: Suppose you received the validation you needed.
What would you feel?
(RSQ) C: Better.
(CAP) T: Help yourself feel better there.
(Collision) Explicit statement of structurally opposite candidate needs (e.g. accompaniment vs. solitude) is an explicit safeguard against therapist leading.
It helps the patient to navigate by internal affective contrast, not by therapist compliance (Ronen-Setter & Cohen, 2020).
text.formatted: It helps the patient to navigate by internal affective contrast, not by therapist compliance (Ronen-Setter & Cohen, 2020).

text.text: The SUD dropped to 5 and the dominant affect was powerlessness.
Cycle 3 (SUD 5 → 3).
This cycle shows the resistant response.
The patient's UAP was the need to hit back.
The Resolved-State Query indicated an empowered state based on retaliatory action.
T: Powerlessness is a sign you needed what?
(UAP) C: To be able to fight back.
T: Suppose you were able to fight back there.
What would you feel?
(RSQ) C: That I had made him pay. (retaliatory ideation) The act was not approved by the therapist.
Further, the Resolved-State Query looked beyondthe act to identify the affective need behind the act.
T: Imagine you made him pay already.
What feeling would ensue?
(RSQ) C: Phew.
And that I am not a weak one.
T: (psychoeducation) It seems that what your system is craving is the relief and the feeling that you are not weak, rather than the act itself.
When that relief is fully there, and that sense that you are not weak is fully there, the push to act may disappear.
The empowered scenario was played out in the imagination.
The client was then returned to the original memory to evaluate the cycle.
The SUD went to 3 and anger was the main affect.
T: Return to the original memory. 0 neutral and 10 most distressing.
Where are you now?
(SUD) C: Three.
C: Anger.
I did it, but I am still angry.
T: What keeps the anger there?
(downward arrow) C: Because in reality nothing has changed.

They are still out there. (obstacle belief) "Reality has not changed" was a hyper-precise prior: the belief that internal revision could only occur once external reality had been corrected (Krupnik, 2020).
text.formatted: They are still out there. (obstacle belief) "Reality has not changed" was a hyper-precise prior: the belief that internal revision could only occur once external reality had been corrected <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Krupnik, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It was a defiant answer.
The system clung to precision in self-defence, unwilling to revise.
The therapist distanced the confrontation, treating the belief as a separate target for intervention and recompressing it into a workable DAS.
T: When you say reality has not changed, what is the dominant feeling in that?
(recompression to a belief-based DAS) C: That it is unfair.
(DAS) T: Unfairness is a sign you needed what?
(UAP) C: To accept it, because in reality it was unfair.
Maybe to grieve that it was unfair.
T: Suppose, there, you had already finished grieving and had accepted that it was unfair.
What would you feel?
(RSQ)
The UAP embraced acceptance and sadness about unfairness.
The RSQ yielded relief as the CAP.
No alteration in external reality was required for this corrective anticipation.
The blockage melted, allowing the cycle to be completed.
The SUD remained 3, and the dominant affect shifted to worthlessness, the conviction that had organised the patient's presentation from the start.
Finally, we used future-pacing to test whether the change generalised beyond this one memory.

The test used a neutral cue that had become associated with the event, not the threatening scene itself (to have the client imagine the threat again could trigger the old prediction and risk re-traumatization).
T: Is there something ordinary in daily life that used to bring this memory back?
C: The smell of the cologne he wore.
Sometimes a stranger on the train wears it.
T: Imagine a day next week.
You are on the train, and someone near you is wearing that cologne.
Notice what happens in your body. (future pacing) C: I notice the smell.
I think, oh, that cologne.
Then I go back to reading my phone.
T: From 0 to 10, how distressing is it?
(SUD) C: Zero.
I just notice it.

The session met the termination criteria of the framework: SUD was zero, there was no negative affect, and the memory was less vivid and more clearly time-stamped, so that the event was experienced as having happened in the past, rather than a present re-experience.
These changes are consistent with the reconsolidation account, but do not confirm it.
Two other signs were the VoC rating and the future pacing test, which indicated that the associated belief had weakened and that the change had generalised to a related cue.
Both were observed within the session.
The generalisation in everyday life has to be judged in the follow up.
SUDs went down in steps for 4 cycles (10 → 7 → 5 → 3 → 0).
Dominant affect shifted (fear → sadness → powerlessness → anger → unfairness → worthlessness).
This is the serialisation of a broad prior.
In each cycle an affective dimension was picked out, paired with a corrective prediction, and the two were brought into collision.
Then came the next dimension.
The case has three aspects that fit the framework.
First, the inert response is evidenced by the failure to form a CAP in Cycle 2: the prediction error was misdirected and thus, no revision happened and the UAP was re-navigated.

Second, the obstacle belief in Cycle 3 shows the resistant response: the system received prediction error but a defensive increase in precision was produced and the belief was treated as a contingent branch.
Third, the end combination of reduced vividness and time-stamping is consistent with the proposal that successful reconsolidation may alter the precision of the prior itself (Monfils & Holmes, 2018).

text.text: Like the present vignette, these reports cannot separate reconsolidation from expectancy or alliance effects.
The above case did not involve overwhelm.
If the patient becomes overwhelmed during processing, the therapist stops the processing and brings the client back to the stabilisation phase.
Processing only resumes when the patient is back within their window of tolerance.
This paper presents Trauma Processing Therapy as a closed-loop protocol designed to manipulate precision-weighted prediction error in destabilized trauma representations.
The discussion compares TPT with related reconsolidation-informed and imagery-based therapies and outlines its limitations and future research needs.
TPT shares conceptual and procedural features with several established therapeutic modalities.

text.text: TPT works on the affect and beliefs within a specific episodic memory, starting from the DAS.

TPT does not use a dual-attention stimulus.
The element activated together with the trauma memory is the CAP.

text.text: TPT assumes that the traumatic prior can be accessed via the episodic memory in which it was created, where emotion and belief are reactivated together.
This assumption is in line with evidence that reactivated episodic memories undergo reconsolidation and can incorporate new information.
It does not mean that working at the episodic level is more effective.
The two approaches may be suited to different clinical presentations.
TPT also uses client-directed imagined scenarios, as does imagery rescripting (IR) (Arntz, 2025).

In TPT, the intervention is the collision, and imagery is just one way to evoke the CAP.

The difference from emotion-focused therapy (EFT) is a basic assumption about emotion.

This overlap leads to a fair question: should TPT be viewed as a distinct protocol?

What might be distinctive is that it couples a particular unit of analysis (the DAS), a structured therapist role, a contrast gated collision and closed-loop calibration that discriminates inert from resistant responses.
When we refer to TPT as a different protocol, we only mean this organization.
It doesn't mean that TPT is more effective than existing approaches, or that it operates through a new mechanism.
There are no controlled outcome data for TPT, only one composite vignette to support the proposed protocol, and efficacy and mechanisms are not established.
The vignette illustrates the order of the protocol, but cannot separate the proposed reconsolidation mechanism from expectancy, therapeutic alliance, or other common factors.

text.text: Therefore, at the end of each cycle the patient returns to the original memory as remembered, and SUD is re-rated against that memory, not against the imagined scenario.
The aim of this step is the prevention of imagined material replacing the original event, but its protective effect has not been tested and cannot remove suggestibility or memory distortion.
Finally, how well TPT generalises is unknown.
It has not been tested across trauma types or populations, especially those with complex trauma, developmental trauma, or dissociative presentations.

These conditions may be associated with different patterns of emotion regulation and memory processing that make trauma-focused work more difficult (Beutler et al., 2022; Cloître et al., 2011), or may be less useful for them.

text.text: Controlled studies are required to test outcomes, mechanisms and safeguards and to define when TPT can be used.
Research on TPT could proceed in phases: early-phase studies first, followed by studies testing effectiveness.
The first step is a treatment manual that describes each stage, the decision rules and safety procedures, as well as measures of therapist adherence and fidelity.
Then a training program can be developed and tested to see if therapists can learn the protocol and deliver it as intended.
Feasibility studies may assess the delivery of the protocol in routine settings including recruitment, retention, session length and adverse events.
Acceptability should be evaluated from two perspectives: clients' tolerance and utility of the procedure, and therapists' usability and compatibility of the procedure with their practice.
Interviews with both groups may suggest what aspects of the protocol need to be changed before larger trials.

The case reports to date used a single session (Ardian, 2025) and six weekly sessions (Octaviani et al., 2026), so feasibility studies should record session number and dose alongside outcomes, and later trials should compare brief with multi-session delivery.

text.text: Mechanistic studies follow because they require a stable, manualized protocol.

We can test whether improvement after TPT is associated with changes consistent with memory reconsolidation using psychophysiological and neuroimaging studies, and whether reduced vividness and time-stamping predict lower physiological reactivity and lasting improvement.
However, reliable human markers of memory destabilisation and reconsolidation are still difficult to establish (Milton et al., 2023; Phelps & Hofmann, 2019).

text.text: These studies would test the central proposal of TPT that long-lasting change depends on calibrated, precision-weighted prediction error during the reconsolidation window, and whether existing learning processes can account for the same changes.

This paper starts with two issues in trauma treatment: the re-emergence of symptoms after extinction-based approaches (Vervliet et al., 2013), and the lack of established conditions for reliable memory updating in reconsolidation research (Phelps & Hofmann, 2019).

text.text: Trauma Processing Therapy (TPT) is a predictive-processing-informed protocol conceptualising trauma as a hyperprecise prior and therapeutic change as calibrated, precision-weighted prediction error while the memory is labile.
It does this in a closed loop of identifying the dominant affective state, evoking a corrective prediction, activating both together, and evaluating change against the original memory.
TPT employs existing therapeutic procedures and arranges them around this loop, with explicit criteria for when to continue and when to stop.
Its efficacy and mechanisms of action have not yet been determined.
The next step is early-phase research on the manual, therapist training, feasibility and acceptability to clients and therapists.

Only then can controlled trials determine whether TPT effects are lasting and mechanistic studies determine whether those effects reflect memory updating or processes already explained by existing learning accounts.
Until then TPT remains a clinical proposition and its value depends upon this evidence.
